subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Dictator Game
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Dictator Game usable.

hook.text: You get $10 to share. The other person must accept whatever you give. No rejection possible. Average gift: $2.80.

buildup.text: The dictator game removes punishment. The receiver can't reject. Standard theory predicts the dictator keeps everything.

discovery.text: Most dictators give something. Social norms, guilt, and intrinsic fairness preferences drive giving even when there's.

twist.text: When dictators are anonymous and believe the receiver can't identify them, giving drops sharply.

climax.text: The dictator game shows that generosity exists but is fragile. Remove observation and social pressure, and giving.

punchline.text: We give partly because someone is watching.

quiz.question: What happens when dictators are made fully anonymous?
options: They give more because guilt increases

details.summary: In the dictator game, one player divides a sum of money with no ability for the receiver to reject the offer. Despite having no strategic reason to share, most dictators give 20 to 30 percent of the total, revealing genuine altruistic preferences.
details.whyItMatters: The dictator game isolates pure generosity from strategic considerations. The consistent finding that people share when they have no reason to disproves the pure self-interest assumption of classical economics.
takeaways: Dictators typically give 20 to 30 percent despite no enforcement mechanism
The game demonstrates genuine other-regarding preferences
Anonymity reduces but does not eliminate giving

faq.question: What does the dictator game tell us about human nature?
faq.answer: People are not purely selfish. Even when they can keep everything with zero consequences, most share. This reveals baseline altruism that exists independently of strategic incentives, reciprocity expectations, or punishment threats.

faq.question: Do experimental conditions change dictator game giving?
faq.answer: Significantly. Double-blind anonymity reduces giving. Earning the money reduces giving. Showing a picture of the recipient increases it. Social distance, framing, and context all modulate the baseline generosity impulse.
